title: The setup around a task
summary: A task comes with a setup, and the setup is something you can describe and ask questions about.
body:
## Setup is part of the task

Every task comes with a setup. How clear are the instructions? Do you get to choose how to do it? Is it noisy? Is anyone nearby? How much time do you have? Do you have tools or help? Is part of it unclear? All of this is the setup, or the **operating conditions**. Setup can change how a task goes without saying anything final about you. If a task goes badly in one setup, that does not tell you what you can or cannot do.

## Say it in concrete words

Concrete beats vague. 'I had a written example' tells you what was there. 'I need structure' is a big phrase that could mean many things. You can keep the big phrase as a **question** to look into, but it is not yet a rule about you. When you describe a condition, name what you could see or hear or count. That gives you something to compare later.

## Watch what happened, then what you made of it

Say what happened first: 'I asked fewer questions when I had the example.' Then notice any bigger claim: 'Written examples always work best for me.' One try cannot support that bigger claim. Keeping the two apart is the whole skill here. You do not have to use anything personal. A made-up task, a task you watch someone else do, or the word-sorting task in the lesson is just as good.

> Imagined example, not a real person: two people do the same ten-minute sorting job. One gets clear categories and a sample. The other gets half the instructions. The second person struggles more. That does not mean they are less able. The setup was different.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Changing one thing, safely
summary: A small, safe change to a task can show you something, if you plan a limit and a stop rule first.
body:
## One change, kept small

A **changed-condition test** means changing one thing about a task. You might write the steps down, cut a distraction, use a tool, slow the pace, or work next to someone. Pick a change that is safe and easy to get. Keep the task about the same size each time, so a short job is compared with a short job. Do not add pressure or take something away to make a point. That does not teach you anything useful.

## Plan the limit and the stop rule

Before you start, write two things. A **time limit** is how long you will spend. A **stop rule** is what will make you end or change course sooner, such as feeling worse or needing to get back to something important. Stopping at your rule is using your plan, not failing it. Also decide what you will notice: fewer questions, easier restarts, how tired you feel after. 'Feeling better' should not be the only thing that counts.

## Hold the result loosely

Even a clear result does not prove the change caused it. You may have gotten better with practice, slept well, or had fewer interruptions. Write those down as other possible reasons. Planning without trying is a real result too. So is 'I had no chance to try.' If you do try, your conclusion is a draft that can change.

> Imagined example, not a real person: someone plans to alphabetize three words twice, once from a paragraph and once from a checklist, for two minutes each. Their stop rule is 'stop if I start feeling tense.' They note that the second try may be easier just because they know the words now.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: What it did, and what it took
summary: Look at both the result and the cost, and say your conclusion as a draft.
body:
## Result and cost together

Finishing a task is useful to know. It does not tell the whole story. Look also at the time, effort, tiredness, and support you needed, during and after. Someone might finish faster with another person nearby and need quiet time afterward. 'It helped me finish and it took energy' is more accurate than 'I should always work with people.' One result can hold a benefit and a cost at the same time.

## Keep a guess separate from what you saw

Say what changed, what happened, and what else was different. Then name your explanation as an explanation. If the second try went smoother, practice may be part of the reason. You are allowed to leave it as 'I don't know which.' That is more honest than picking one.

## A draft note, and your choice

A good note sounds like this: 'For this task, in these conditions, I noticed this result and this cost.' It is not a type or a permanent preference. Then you choose: keep it, change it, test again, pause, stop, go another way, or keep looking. A small note and an open question are enough.

> Imagined example, not a real person: someone finishes a task sooner with a friend nearby, but feels worn out afterward. Their note: 'With a friend nearby, I finished sooner. It cost me quiet time later. I do not know yet if that is true for other tasks.'
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Event, story, verdict
summary: What happened, what you made of it, and what you decided about yourself are three different things.
body:
## Three pieces

The **event** is what happened. You could point to it or check it. The **story** is your explanation. It might be right, partly right, or off. A **verdict** is a big judgment about who you are. And some parts are **unknown**, because you haven't checked yet. Pulling them apart does not make a hard moment positive. It makes it more accurate.

## Responsibility stays

Looking closely does not let anyone off the hook. You can say 'I missed the deadline,' admit it mattered, and still ask what the instructions said or what skill you need. You also do not have to swap a harsh verdict for a flattering one. Aim for a sentence that fits the facts and can be changed.

## A revised sentence

Try: 'I missed this deadline. I need to check the instructions and decide what to do differently.' That sentence gives you something to do. You can use a made-up example or a plain everyday one. You never need to share anything personal, and this is a thinking tool, not therapy.

> Imagined example, not a real person: Event: someone stopped an activity after 20 minutes. Story: 'I can't handle hard things.' Verdict: 'I never follow through.' A more accurate sentence: 'I stopped after 20 minutes when the room got hard to work in. I don't know the whole reason yet.'
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: From a value to a small action
summary: Pick something that matters to you and find one small action you could actually see yourself take.
body:
## Value, standard, practice

A **value** is something that matters to you. A **standard** is what that value asks in one situation. A **practice** is a small action you can see. Value: accuracy. Standard: check a message before passing it on. Practice: ask which version is the current one. You can tell if the practice happened. You do not have to rate how accurate a person you are.

## Whose value is it?

Check that the value is yours, not one you picked up from the program, a facilitator, family, a boss, or a group. It is fine if it is shared. You just want to know. Then think of a cue, like feeling pulled to rush when you see a deadline. Use cues from normal life. Do not make pressure on purpose.

## Plan with room

Write the cue, the action, a limit, and when to stop. A week is a window to notice a chance, not a promise that one will come. If none comes, write 'no chance.' Asking for help, using support, setting a boundary, doing part of it, or choosing not to continue all count as real evidence.

> Imagined example, not a real person: value, respect. Standard: ask before giving advice. Practice: before offering help, ask 'Do you want ideas, help, or just someone to listen?'
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Revising what you say
summary: When you learn something new, you can change your wording to match, without having to sound positive.
body:
## Revise to fit, not to cheer up

Revising means changing your wording because new information changes what you can fairly say. It is not a push to be more positive. Keep the old wording where you can see it. Then put the new evidence next to it. Suppose the old statement was 'I never ask for help.' After asking once, a fair revision is: 'I asked for help in this situation. I don't know yet what makes it easier or harder elsewhere.'

## Parts can go different ways

Some evidence supports part of a statement and challenges another part. Note the chance you had, what you did, the conditions, and the cost. Practised, partly practised, missed with a chance, no chance, not tried, and unknown are descriptions, not marks. If no chance came up, there may be nothing new to say yet. That is fine.

## Pick one thing to carry

If you want, pick one observation or one possible next step to keep. You decide what stays private. A review like this does not diagnose anything or change who you are. It just makes your wording a bit more accurate.

> Imagined example, not a real person: Earlier statement: 'I never ask for help.' Observation: 'I asked someone to explain the instructions.' Revised: 'I asked for help here. I don't know yet what would happen with a different task or person.' It does not become 'I always ask for help.'
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Looking at a moment in pieces
summary: One way to look at a moment is as five pieces: signal, story, urge, usual action, and cost.
body:
## Five pieces, any of them optional

A **signal** is something you notice in your body, attention, pace, or energy. A **story** is the meaning you give the moment. An **urge** is a pull to do or avoid something. The **usual action** is what you often do next. The **cost** is what that takes: time, effort, energy, or a responsibility you had to drop. Not everyone sees five neat steps. Any piece can be missing or unknown.

## An imagined moment

Imagined example: an instruction is unclear. The person notices they are rereading faster (signal). They think 'I should already get this' (story). They feel pulled to rush (urge). They submit without checking (action). Fixing it later takes extra time (cost). This is made up. It is not a diagnosis and does not explain every rushed task.

## Maps are for choice, not calm

Noticing a signal does not tell you its cause. You can also map a time when things went well and see what helped. The goal is to keep a choice open, not to make you calm. You do not need to breathe a certain way, close your eyes, move, or feel a certain thing. This is a learning tool. It is not treatment and not crisis care.

> Imagined example, not a real person: reading an unclear instruction. Signal: rereading faster. Story: 'I should already understand this.' Urge: to rush. Action: submit without checking. Cost: extra time to fix it later.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Two equal routes
summary: You can protect something that already works, or try one small, reversible response. Both count.
body:
## Route A: protect what works

You don't need a setback to learn something. **Route A** is about **continuation**. Notice a condition that helps you stay with a task in a way that feels chosen and flexible. Maybe clear instructions or a stopping time. Ask what you want to keep, whether you can stop and come back, and what would protect it. The result can be one working condition and a decision to continue.

## Route B: one small response

**Route B** is **navigation**. Pick something practical you can undo. You could ask what an instruction means. You could write one next action or make the job smaller. You could ask for one kind of help, take an agreed break, or change where you sit. You could stop safely or plan to return later. Before you try it, say what a useful next choice would look like. It might be understanding a limit or deciding to stop. It does not have to be calm.

## Use real chances, keep it loose

Use things that come up on their own. Do not create urgency or count episodes. Notice what happened later as well as right away. A change after a response does not prove the response caused it. Stopping or going another way is not failing. If anything gets heavier or gets in the way of a responsibility, stop and use your support.

> Imagined example, not a real person: Route A. Someone notices a stopping time keeps their afternoon free, and decides to keep it. Route B. Someone with a confusing task asks, 'Which part do I do first?' and writes that one step down.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Impression, evidence, and what you keep
summary: A hunch can be a good question. Check what backs it up, and choose what to keep.
body:
## A hunch is a starting point

An **impression** is a hunch, like 'this kind of task suits me.' It can point to a good question. It is not the same as evidence. Ask what supports it, what challenges it, and what you don't know. One session of staying interested with clear instructions and support is worth keeping. It doesn't tell you how the task would feel in other conditions.

## A rule and a boundary

A **decision rule** names what will guide your next choice, such as 'I'll try again if it fits in this time and doesn't get in the way of work.' A **protected boundary** names what you don't want the next step to cost. Neither is a business plan. Neither is forever.

## Closing Pilot 1

If you want, look back at four things: a piece of evidence, a condition or strategy worth keeping, a support that mattered, and one question for later. Keep, change, test again, pause, stop, another direction, and keep looking are all fine. Nothing carries on automatically, and nobody is judging if you are ready.

> Imagined example, not a real person: Impression: 'A shorter instruction must be easier.' Evidence: the paragraph and checklist hold the same three steps. A bounded question: 'Does a checklist help me follow this task?' Limit: 10 minutes, with permission to stop.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: A small question you can check
summary: A good first question is small enough to look into, and you do not need to defend it.
body:
## Start with curiosity

You can be curious about a job, a course, a trade, a project, or a problem. You can also start with an honest unknown. Nobody asks you to pitch an idea or promise to fix anything. A question lets you look first and decide later.

## Make it small

Some questions are too big to answer. "Is this my future?" is one of them. A smaller one gives you something to check: "What does a beginner actually do in this field?" or "What are the hours and requirements for this course?" Small does not mean unimportant. It means you can find an answer with what you can reach now.

## Pick a way to learn

You might read public information, look at program materials, watch a class video, or ask someone who is willing to talk. Reaching out to people is optional. A practice scenario can help you think, but it does not show you what a real workplace is like. Also name what your source can and cannot tell you.

> Imagined example: someone is interested in cooking work. A big question: "Will I love professional kitchens?" A small question: "What does a first taste of culinary training involve?" The small one can be checked this week.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Six labels for what you find
summary: Labeling what you find helps you see what it does and does not show.
body:
## Different kinds of information

Not everything you find is the same kind of thing. Something you saw yourself is different from something a person told you. Published facts are different again. Labels help you notice which is which, so nothing quietly becomes proof of more than it shows.

## The six labels

Direct observation: you saw it or could check it. Secondhand report: someone else described it. Existing information: published hours, costs, rules, or data. Assumption: something you believe but have not checked. Conclusion: your own interpretation for now. Uncertainty: something still unknown or out of reach.

## What one source cannot do

One person's story tells you what that person said. It does not tell you how common it is. A web page may be out of date, so note its date. If you hear nothing back, or cannot get access, write that down. A blank is an outcome. It is not a gap to fill with a guess. Ask permission before taking notes or sharing what someone says.

> Imagined example: a program page lists evening classes three times a week (existing information). A graduate says the kitchen is fast-paced (secondhand report). "I will love this" is an assumption until tried.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Three equal ways to look
summary: You can look at a pathway, a problem, or keep exploring, and none is the real one.
body:
## Three branches

A branch helps you focus. It is not a ranking. A pathway branch looks at a job, course, trade, creative work, service, or another direction you name. A problem branch looks at a friction, a delay, or a missing service. A keep-exploring branch compares options, repeats a small look, or pauses. All three are equally fine, and business is not the real track.

## What to ask

On a pathway, ask what the work involves and which requirements are real. Comparing a course schedule with your actual week checks fit better than imagining an ideal week. On a problem, ask who runs into it, when, who bears the cost, and whose view is missing. A repeated complaint can suggest a question. It does not prove anyone would pay for a fix.

## What you end with

You end with a short evidence note and a next choice. You do not need an offer or a verdict. A learning conversation is not formal research, treatment, or a job. Keep private or identifying details out unless there is an approved process for them.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Fit and a reversible decision
summary: Outside facts and personal fit are two questions, and you can answer them separately.
body:
## Two questions

"Is this real out there?" and "does this fit my life?" are different. Liking an activity does not show that anyone needs it. A promising course may still clash with your hours, energy, or responsibilities. Check one practical detail where you can: hours, eligibility, cost, location, transport.

## Hold all the facts

An accurate conclusion can hold several facts at once. For example: the course interests me, the entry rules are clear, and the timetable does not work. That is not failure. You might look at another format, park it, or look somewhere else. Interest does not oblige you to enrol. If you are on the problem branch, ask whether evidence supports the problem, whether you want to look into it, and whether the demands are workable. No scores.

## A reversible decision

Your discovery decision can be Continue, Redefine, Research, Park, Stop, Another Direction, or Continue Looking. Each is a full decision. A next try is optional, and you do not have to move to the next module. Name what would make you revise it.

> Imagined example: a person finds a course they like, with clear entry rules but only daytime classes, and they work days. Their note: "Fits my interest; does not fit my hours; unknown whether an evening option exists." Decision: Research.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)
